summary: Defines a P-Served-User header field parameter for an originating call diversion session case in SIP. The header comes from 3GPP IMS requirements to convey the served user's identity, registration state and session case.

eli5.summary: A phone system needs to know whose call is whose. This adds a tag for a call that was forwarded.

questions: what is a session case in ims
how does sip call diversion work
subtitle: A new SIP header parameter that tells a network which kind of session a forwarded call leg is.

tldr.problem: When a call is diverted, the new call leg is not a true originating call from the diverting user, yet the existing session cases cannot say so, so the right services cannot be triggered.
tldr.mechanism: The P-Served-User header field gets a new session case parameter, orig-cdiv, which the S-CSCF sets after a diversion so that an application server can run the diverting user's originating-after-CDIV services.
tldr.outcome: The parameter is only for use inside a trust domain. The RFC also fixes the ABNF of RFC 5502 and clarifies how the header is handled.

today: RFC 8498 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 5502 by adding the orig-cdiv parameter and correcting its ABNF.

sections.title: Background and the Problem
sections.content:
The P-Served-User header field from RFC 5502 came from a requirement of the 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS). It carries the identity of the served user, the registration state, and the session case between a Serving Call Session Control Function (S-CSCF) and an Application Server (AS). A session case is metadata about the session, whether or not the user is registered and whether the session originates or terminates with the served user.

The S-CSCF is a SIP proxy that acts as registrar and handles originating and terminating sessions for its users. It downloads the user profile from the Home Subscriber Server (HSS) and uses it, with filter criteria, to decide whether to send a request to an AS.

The problem arises with Call Diversion (CDIV). In the RFC's example, Alice calls Bob, and Bob has a diversion to Carol. The request is first treated as terminating at Bob. The AS changes the Request-URI to Carol and a new leg is created. It looks like an originating call from Bob, but the originating user is still Alice. Bob's privacy service should not hide Alice's identity, for example. Without a dedicated session case, the S-CSCF cannot trigger Bob's originating services for this leg.
sections.eli5: If Bob forwards Alice's call to Carol, it is still Alice's call. The phone system needs a way to say 'this is Bob's forwarded call' so it does not mix up the rules.

sections.title: How a Proxy Uses orig-cdiv
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a terminating call. The S-CSCF receives the INVITE, determines the served user from the Request-URI and saves it, then sends the request to the AS with sescase=term and a regstate value. The AS decides to divert, replaces the Request-URI with the new address, records history in History-Info entries, and returns the INVITE to the S-CSCF.

When the S-CSCF sees its own hostname in the top Route header but a Request-URI that no longer matches the saved one, it replaces the sescase parameter with orig-cdiv. The header value is otherwise unchanged. The S-CSCF then forwards the request to an AS that hosts the diverting user's originating services, and that AS performs them for the orig-cdiv case.

Use is applicable only inside a Trust Domain (RFC 3324), where nodes trust each other to convey the served user and withhold that information outside the domain.
sections.eli5: After the call is forwarded, the switchboard notices the destination changed and stamps the call 'forwarded'. The next helper then knows which rules to follow.

sections.title: Clarifications to RFC 5502
sections.content:
This RFC updates RFC 5502 with guidance the earlier text lacked. The P-Served-User header field MUST NOT be repeated within a request for a session, and MUST NOT contain multiple values, either comma-separated or header-separated, because session cases are mutually exclusive.

RFC 5502 also did not say what to do with the header when a call is diverted. The RFC lists several choices: keep the previous regstate, remove it because it may no longer be relevant, or combine it with orig-cdiv to give different services to registered and unregistered users. These choices are implementation dependent.
sections.eli5: The rules now say a call can have only one stamp at a time, and they list a few ways to handle the old registration note.

sections.title: Syntax and Examples
sections.content:
The sessioncase-param previously allowed sescase with orig or term. This RFC adds orig-cdiv in a way that fits the parameter format of 3GPP Release 11 and remains backward compatible. It also corrects errors found in the ABNF of RFC 5502.

The name-addr form, with angle brackets, MUST be used if the addr-spec would contain a comma, question mark or semicolon. Valid headers include P-Served-User: <sip:user@example.com>; orig-cdiv; regstate=reg and P-Served-User: <sip:user@example.com>; sescase=term; regstate=unreg.

The RFC includes call flows for a diversion when Bob is busy, with a 486 response, and a second flow showing diversion with privacy.
sections.eli5: The tag has a strict spelling. The new tag is spelled orig-cdiv, and the rules fix a few typos from the old spelling guide.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA updated the P-Served-User row in the SIP header field registry to reference both RFC 5502 and RFC 8498. It also added rows in the header field parameters registry for sescase and regstate (with predefined values) and orig-cdiv (no predefined values).

The security considerations of RFC 5502 apply. Because orig-cdiv can trigger applications on a diverted call, it must not be added by an unauthorized SIP entity. The header is for a trusted environment, and proxies MUST NOT insert it unless they know the route set includes another trusted proxy.
sections.eli5: Only trusted switchboards may add the forwarded stamp, otherwise someone could trick the system into running the wrong services.
